title: 23 Things They Don't Tell You About Capitalism
author: Ha-Joon Chang
target_audience: General readers interested in economics and society
Students of economics, politics, and business
Professionals seeking a critical perspective on capitalism
core_themes: Myths and misconceptions of mainstream economics
Role of government in the economy
primary_purpose: To demystify commonly accepted beliefs about capitalism by exposing key myths perpetuated by orthodox economics, making complex economic ideas accessible to lay readers, and challenging the notion that unregulated markets always lead to prosperity.

structure_format.organization: Divided into 23 short chapters—each one discussing a specific 'thing' or myth, presented with supporting evidence and counter-arguments
features: Summary of key lessons at the end of each chapter
Suggestions for re-thinking policy and economic priorities

key_concepts_lessons: There is no such thing as a perfectly free market; markets are always shaped by rules and restrictions.
Despite popular belief, capitalism did not make all countries rich; historical development policies were far from laissez-faire.
The rich are not necessarily more entrepreneurial; inherited wealth and systemic advantages play bigger roles than acknowledged.
Globalization does not always benefit poor countries; the process is uneven and structured by power imbalances.
Equality of opportunity is not enough; outcomes matter, and real social mobility requires intervention.
Greater government intervention often correlates with higher economic growth.
Managers are not always motivated by maximizing shareholder value; social, cultural, and psychological drives also influence economic agents.
notable_features: Each chapter debunks a widely held economic myth
Emphasizes the role of history and context in shaping economies
Presents alternative economic perspectives rooted in heterodox economics
cultural_historical_context: Published in the aftermath of the 2008 global financial crisis, the book reflects renewed skepticism toward unregulated markets. It critiques neoliberalism and free-market dogma which have dominated mainstream economics since the late 20th century, echoing growing public debates about inequality and the social costs of unchecked capitalism.
reception_impact: Praised for making economic debates accessible to a broad readership
Influential among students, activists, and critics of neoliberalism
Cited in academic and policy debates about market regulation
Some critics argue the book oversimplifies complex issues or underestimates the benefits of market reforms
comparable_titles: Capital in the Twenty-First Century by Thomas Piketty
The Shock Doctrine by Naomi Klein
The End of Alchemy by Mervyn King
The Globalization Paradox by Dani Rodrik
